modules.title: 1. What Is a Push-Up? Purpose and Muscles Involved
modules.content:
## A Simple Way to Ask “What Is a Push‑Up?”

Imagine you’re standing in line at a coffee shop. The person in front of you leans forward, lowers their body, then pushes back up again—no equipment, no weights, just their own body. That movement is the classic **push‑up**. It’s a tiny, self‑contained exercise that anyone can do almost anywhere, and yet it’s powerful enough to build strength, improve posture, and boost everyday performance.

If you’ve never tried one, or if the name sounds like a gymnastics term you can’t quite picture, you’re in the right place. Below we’ll break down **what a push‑up actually is**, **which muscles do the work**, and **why adding it to your routine is a smart move**.

---

## 1. Defining the Push‑Up in Plain Language

A **push‑up** is a body‑weight movement where you start in a straight, plank‑like position, **lower your chest toward the floor**, and then **press back up** to the starting position. The whole motion is performed using the muscles of your upper body and core, while your feet stay planted on the ground.

### Key Elements of a Standard Push‑Up

| Element | What It Looks Like | Why It Matters |
|---------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Starting Position** | Hands placed shoulder‑width apart on the floor, arms straight, body forming a straight line from head to heels. | Sets the foundation for a safe, efficient movement. |
| **Descent (Eccentric Phase)** | Bend the elbows, chest moves toward the floor while keeping the body rigid. | Controls the load and engages the target muscles. |
| **Ascent (Concentric Phase)** | Extend the elbows, pushing the body back to the start. | Generates strength and builds muscle. |
| **Alignment** | Head, spine, and hips remain in one plane; no sagging hips or piking shoulders. | Protects the lower back and shoulders. |

> **Note:** The term *eccentric* describes the muscle‑lengthening part of a movement (lowering), while *concentric* describes the muscle‑shortening part (lifting).

---

## 2. The Major Muscle Groups at Work

When you push your body up, several muscle groups cooperate. Understanding who does what helps you see why a push‑up is more than just a chest exercise.

### 2.1 Primary Movers (the “big engines”)

| Muscle | Location | Role in the Push‑Up |
|--------|----------|---------------------|
| **Pectoralis Major** | Front of the chest | Main driver that pushes the arms forward and together. |
| **Triceps Brachii** | Back of the upper arm | Straightens the elbow, completing the press back up. |
| **Anterior Deltoid** | Front of the shoulder | Assists the chest and triceps in moving the arm forward. |

### 2.2 Secondary Support Muscles (the “assistants”)

| Muscle | Location | Contribution |
|--------|----------|--------------|
| **Serratus Anterior** | Side of the rib cage, under the shoulder blade | Keeps the shoulder blades flat against the back, stabilizing the shoulder joint. |
| **Core Muscles** (rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, obliques) | Mid‑section of the torso | Maintain a rigid, straight line; prevent hips from sagging or piking. |
| **Latissimus Dorsi** | Upper back, sides | Helps control the descent and adds stability to the shoulder joint. |
| **Gluteus Maximus** | Buttocks | Locks the hips, contributing to overall body rigidity. |

> **Why “muscle groups” matter:** If one group is weak or inactive, the others must compensate, which can lead to poor form or injury. A balanced push‑up engages all of the above, promoting overall functional strength.

### 2.3 A Quick Visual Checklist

- **Chest (Pectorals)** – *pushes forward*  
- **Arms (Triceps & Front Shoulders)** – *extends elbows*  
- **Shoulder Blades (Serratus)** – *holds blades flat*  
- **Core (Abs & Obliques)** – *keeps body straight*  
- **Back (Lats)** – *guides arm path*  
- **Glutes** – *locks hips*

---

## 3. Why Push‑Ups Deserve a Spot in Your Routine

Beyond the obvious “it works the chest,” push‑ups bring a suite of benefits that ripple through everyday life.

### 3.1 Functional Strength

*Functional* means the strength you use in real‑world tasks—lifting groceries, pushing a door, or getting up from a low seat. Because a push‑up mimics the natural pushing motion, the strength you gain translates directly to daily activities.

### 3.2 Minimal Equipment, Maximum Flexibility

- **No gear needed** – just a flat surface.
- **Scalable** – from wall push‑ups to one‑arm variations, you can adjust the difficulty without buying anything.
- **Portable** – you can do them in a living room, park, hotel room, or office break area.

### 3.3 Joint‑Friendly Conditioning

When performed with proper form, push‑ups strengthen the muscles that **stabilize the shoulder joint** and **protect the elbow**. Strong, well‑coordinated muscles reduce the risk of overuse injuries common in activities that involve pushing or lifting.

### 3.4 Cardiovascular Boost

Doing push‑ups in sets with short rest intervals raises heart rate, giving you a **mini‑cardio workout**. This dual benefit of strength and cardio is especially handy for busy beginners who need efficient training.

### 3.5 Bone Health

Weight‑bearing exercises like push‑ups stimulate bone remodeling, helping to **maintain or increase bone density**—a key factor in preventing osteoporosis later in life.

### 3.6 Mental Gains

- **Confidence:** Mastering a movement that feels challenging at first builds self‑esteem.
- **Focus:** Maintaining a straight line requires concentration, sharpening mind‑body connection.
- **Stress Relief:** Physical exertion releases endorphins, the body’s natural mood elevators.

---

## 4. Putting the Definition and Benefits Together

When you combine the simple description of the movement with the list of engaged muscles and the array of benefits, a clear picture emerges:

> **A push‑up is a versatile, body‑weight exercise that simultaneously trains the chest, arms, shoulders, core, back, and glutes, while delivering functional strength, joint stability, cardiovascular conditioning, and mental confidence—all without any equipment.**

Understanding this “big picture” helps you stay motivated and purposeful as you begin practicing the movement.

---

## 5. Common Questions from Beginners (and Quick Answers)

| Question | Simple Answer |
|----------|---------------|
| **Do I need a special mat?** | No. A clean, flat surface works. A thin yoga mat can add comfort but isn’t required. |
| **Can I do push‑ups if I’m overweight?** | Absolutely. Start with wall or knee variations and progress as you build strength. |
| **Will push‑ups make me “bulky”?** | Unlikely. Building large muscle mass requires specific training and nutrition; push‑ups mainly improve tone and endurance. |
| **How many should I do each session?** | Begin with a set you can complete with good form—often 5‑10 reps. Quality beats quantity. |
| **Is it okay to feel a stretch in my chest on the way down?** | Yes, a mild stretch is normal. Pain, however, signals poor form or over‑stretching and should be avoided. |

---

## 6. Visualizing the Movement: A Step‑by‑Step Walkthrough

1. **Get into the plank position**  
   - Hands under shoulders, fingers spread for stability.  
   - Feet together or a few inches apart, toes planted.  
   - Body forms a straight line from head to heels.

2. **Engage your core**  
   - Pull your belly button toward your spine.  
   - Squeeze your glutes to keep hips from sagging.

3. **Lower yourself**  
   - Bend elbows out to the sides (about a 45‑degree angle).  
   - Keep elbows close to your ribcage—this protects the shoulders.  
   - Stop when your chest is a few inches above the floor (or touches it if you’re comfortable).

4. **Press back up**  
   - Straighten elbows, driving through the palms.  
   - Keep the body rigid; avoid letting hips drop or rise.  

5. **Repeat**  
   - Maintain breathing: inhale on the way down, exhale on the way up.

> **Tip:** If you feel your hips sagging, think about “pushing the floor away with your feet” to keep the line tight.

---

## 7. Quick Reference: Push‑Up Benefits at a Glance

- **Strengthens**: Chest, shoulders, triceps, core, back, glutes.  
- **Improves**: Posture, shoulder stability, functional daily movements.  
- **Boosts**: Heart rate, bone density, mental confidence.  
- **Requires**: No equipment, minimal space, adaptable difficulty.

---

## Key Takeaways

- A **push‑up** is a simple, body‑weight exercise that involves lowering the chest toward the floor and pushing back up while maintaining a straight, plank‑like body line.  
- **Primary muscles**: Pectoralis major, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid. **Secondary muscles**: Serratus anterior, core group, latissimus dorsi, gluteus maximus.  
- Regular push‑up training delivers **functional strength**, **joint stability**, **cardiovascular benefits**, **bone health**, and **mental confidence**, all without any equipment.  
- Beginners should focus on **form**—a rigid body line, controlled descent, and full extension—before increasing repetitions or difficulty.  

By mastering the push‑up, you lay a solid foundation for the rest of your strength‑training journey. Ready to try it? Turn the page and learn how to prepare your body for safe, effective practice.

modules.title: 2. Preparing Your Body: Mobility and Warm-Up
modules.content:
## Warm‑Up: The First Set of Reps for Your Body  

Imagine you’re about to do your first set of push‑ups. You drop into the **Starting Position**, lower your chest toward the floor, and—*snap!*—your wrist hurts. The pain isn’t a sign that you’re “bad” at push‑ups; it’s a warning that the joints that will bear the load haven’t been prepared. A well‑structured warm‑up does three things:  

1. **Increases blood flow** to the muscles that will work during the push‑up (pectoralis major, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid, core, etc.).  
2. **Improves joint range of motion** so you can keep the proper **Alignment** throughout the **Descent** and **Ascent**.  
3. **Reduces the risk of acute injury** by priming the nervous system and lubricating the cartilage in the wrists, shoulders, and thoracic spine.  

The following sections give you a complete, beginner‑friendly 5‑minute dynamic warm‑up that hits each of those goals. No equipment is needed—just a few minutes of space and your own body.

---

## 1. The Science of a Dynamic Warm‑Up  

### 1.1 Dynamic vs. Static Stretching  

| **Dynamic** | **Static** |
|------------|------------|
| Moves joints through their full range of motion (e.g., arm circles). | Holds a stretch for 15–60 seconds without movement. |
| Raises heart rate and body temperature. | Primarily improves flexibility after activity. |
| Improves neuromuscular activation—ideal before strength work. | Can temporarily reduce power if done right before explosive moves. |

Because push‑ups are a **strength** movement that relies on coordinated activation of the chest, shoulders, and core, a **dynamic** warm‑up is the most effective. Static stretching can be saved for the cool‑down phase.

### 1.2 How Warm‑Up Prevents Injury  

- **Synovial fluid** (the lubricating liquid inside joint capsules) increases with movement, allowing smoother joint glide.  
- **Muscle temperature** rises ~1 °C per minute of light activity, which improves muscle elasticity and contractile speed.  
- **Proprioceptive signaling**—the body’s sense of joint position—sharpens, helping you maintain the correct **Alignment** during the push‑up’s eccentric and concentric phases.

---

## 2. The 5‑Minute Dynamic Warm‑Up Routine  

The routine is broken into three blocks: **General Cardio**, **Joint Mobility**, and **Movement‑Specific Activation**. Perform each block in the order listed; the total time should be close to five minutes. Adjust the speed slightly if you need extra time for a particular drill.

### 2.1 Block 1 – General Cardio (≈ 60 seconds)  

Purpose: raise core temperature and get blood flowing to the upper‑body musculature.

| Exercise | How to Do It | Reps / Time |
|----------|--------------|-------------|
| **Jumping Jacks** | Stand tall, feet together, arms at sides. Jump, spreading feet shoulder‑width and raising arms overhead; return to start. | 30 seconds |
| **High Knees** | March or jog in place, driving each knee toward the chest while pumping opposite arms. | 30 seconds |

*Tip:* Keep a light bounce—don’t sprint. The goal is warmth, not fatigue.

### 2.2 Block 2 – Joint Mobility (≈ 120 seconds)  

Focuses on the three key joints for a push‑up: **wrist**, **shoulder**, and **thoracic spine**. Each drill is **dynamic**, meaning you’ll move through the range rather than hold a static stretch.

#### 2.2.1 Wrist Mobility  

1. **Wrist Rolls** – Extend both arms in front of you, palms down. Circle each wrist clockwise for 5 seconds, then counter‑clockwise for 5 seconds.  
2. **Palm‑Up/Down Rock** – With arms extended, rotate each hand so the palm faces up, then down, alternating every 2 seconds.  
3. **Tabletop Reach** – Get into a tabletop position (hands under shoulders, knees under hips). Shift weight forward, allowing the wrists to bend gently while keeping the forearms flat on the floor. Return to neutral. Perform **8–10 repetitions**.

*Why it matters:* Proper wrist extension and flexion allow you to keep the hands flat on the floor without excessive strain on the **wrist joint capsule**.

#### 2.2.2 Shoulder Mobility  

1. **Arm Circles** – Extend arms to the sides, palms down. Small circles for 10 seconds, then gradually enlarge the circles for another 10 seconds. Reverse direction.  
2. **Scapular Wall Slides** – Stand with back against a wall, elbows at 90°, forearms against the wall. Slide arms upward, keeping contact, then return. Perform **10 repetitions**.  
3. **Thoracic “Cat‑Cow”** – From tabletop, inhale, drop belly, lift chest (Cow); exhale, round back (Cat). Move slowly for **10 cycles**.

*Why it matters:* The shoulder joint (glenohumeral joint) and the surrounding **scapular** (shoulder blade) muscles need full, pain‑free motion to keep the **Alignment** stable during the push‑up’s descent.

#### 2.2.3 Thoracic Spine Mobility  

1. **Thread‑the‑Needle** – From tabletop, slide the right arm under the left, lowering the right shoulder toward the floor. Return to start and repeat on the left side. **8–10 reps per side**.  
2. **Standing Thoracic Rotation** – Stand tall, feet hip‑width. Place hands behind head, elbows out. Rotate torso to the right, then left, keeping hips square. **12 rotations** (6 each side).  

*Why it matters:* A mobile thoracic spine lets the shoulder blades **protract** and **retract** smoothly, which is essential for the **Serratus Anterior** to function correctly during push‑ups.

### 2.3 Block 3 – Movement‑Specific Activation (≈ 120 seconds)  

Now we cue the muscles that will actually generate force in a push‑up.

| Exercise | How to Do It | Reps |
|----------|--------------|------|
| **Band‑Assisted Push‑Up Hold** (optional) | Place a light resistance band around the upper back and hold the **Starting Position** for 10 seconds, focusing on tightening the core and keeping the shoulders over the wrists. | 2 sets |
| **Plank Shoulder Taps** | From a high plank (hands under shoulders, body in a straight line), tap the opposite shoulder with each hand, alternating. Keep hips stable. | 12 taps (6 each side) |
| **Chest‑Opener “Y” Raise** | Lie face‑down on the floor, lift arms overhead forming a “Y” while squeezing the shoulder blades together. Hold 2 seconds, lower. | 8 repetitions |

If you don’t have a band, skip the first drill and add an extra set of **Plank Shoulder Taps**.

*Purpose:* These moves reinforce the neural pathways that coordinate the **pectoralis major**, **triceps brachii**, and **core muscles** during the push‑up’s **Eccentric** and **Concentric** phases.

---

## 3. Putting It All Together – Sample Timing  

| **Minute** | **Activity** |
|------------|--------------|
| 0:00–0:30 | Jumping Jacks |
| 0:30–1:00 | High Knees |
| 1:00–1:20 | Wrist Rolls (both directions) |
| 1:20–1:40 | Palm‑Up/Down Rock |
| 1:40–2:00 | Tabletop Wrist Reach (8–10 reps) |
| 2:00–2:30 | Arm Circles (small → large) |
| 2:30–3:00 | Scapular Wall Slides (10 reps) |
| 3:00–3:30 | Cat‑Cow (10 cycles) |
| 3:30–4:00 | Thread‑the‑Needle (8–10 each side) |
| 4:00–4:30 | Standing Thoracic Rotation (12 total) |
| 4:30–4:45 | Plank Shoulder Taps (12 taps) |
| 4:45–5:00 | Chest‑Opener “Y” Raise (8 reps) |

Feel free to adjust the timing (e.g., add a few extra seconds to a drill that feels tight). The key is to finish the routine feeling **warm**, **mobile**, and **ready** to engage the push‑up muscles.

---

## 4. Tips for Consistency and Progression  

- **Micro‑Warm‑Up:** If you’re short on time, do at least the wrist and shoulder drills for 30 seconds each. Even a brief routine beats a cold start.  
- **Progressive Load:** As you become comfortable, increase the range of motion (e.g., larger arm circles) or add a light resistance band to the scapular wall slides.  
- **Breathing Cue:** Inhale during the opening (e.g., during arm circles) and exhale while closing (e.g., during wall slides). Proper breathing helps maintain intra‑abdominal pressure for a stable core.  
- **Environment:** Perform the warm‑up on a non‑slippery surface. A yoga mat or rubber gym floor reduces the chance of slipping during wrist rolls.  
- **Track It:** Keep a simple log—write the date and note any joint discomfort. Over weeks you’ll see patterns and can adjust the routine accordingly.

---

## 5. Common Warm‑Up Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)  

| Mistake | Why It’s Problematic | Quick Fix |
|---------|---------------------|-----------|
| **Skipping the wrist drills** because “they feel easy.” | Wrist joints are often the first to complain during push‑ups; neglecting them leaves you vulnerable to strain. | Treat wrist mobility as non‑negotiable; perform it even if you feel fine. |
| **Holding static stretches** before the push‑up set. | Static stretching can temporarily reduce muscle power and neuromuscular activation. | Replace static holds with the dynamic drills listed above. |
| **Rushing through the mobility drills** (e.g., doing 1‑2 reps). | Inadequate repetitions don’t sufficiently lubricate the joint or cue the nervous system. | Aim for the prescribed reps; if you’re short on time, prioritize quality over speed. |
| **Using too much momentum** (e.g., swinging arms). | Momentum defeats the purpose of controlled joint movement and can mask underlying stiffness. | Move deliberately; think “slow and steady” for each circle or slide. |
| **Neglecting the thoracic spine** because the focus is on arms. | A stiff thoracic spine limits shoulder blade movement, leading to compensations in the shoulders or wrists. | Include at least one thoracic drill each session. |

---

## 6. Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: “Can I do the warm‑up on my knees instead of standing?”**  
A: Yes. For the cardio block, marching in place works just as well. For wrist and shoulder drills, staying on your knees reduces load on the lower body and lets you focus on the upper‑body joints.

**Q: “I have limited mobility in my shoulders—will these drills hurt?”**  
A: The drills are low‑impact and designed to stay within a pain‑free range. If a movement feels sharp, reduce the range (e.g., smaller arm circles) and progress gradually.

**Q: “Do I need a resistance band for the warm‑up?”**  
A: No. The band is optional and only adds a cue for core engagement. The routine works perfectly well without it.

**Q: “How often should I repeat the warm‑up?”**  
A: Every time you practice push‑ups—whether it’s a daily routine or a weekly session. Consistency builds joint health over the long term.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- A **dynamic warm‑up** raises body temperature, improves joint lubrication, and primes the nervous system, dramatically lowering injury risk during push‑ups.  
- The **5‑minute routine** is split into:  
  1. **General cardio** (jumping jacks, high knees) – 60 seconds.  
  2. **Joint mobility** – wrist rolls & reaches, arm circles, scapular wall slides, cat‑cow, thread‑the‑needle, thoracic rotations – ~2 minutes.  
  3. **Movement‑specific activation** – plank shoulder taps and chest‑opener “Y” raises – ~2 minutes.  
- Prioritize **wrist, shoulder, and thoracic** mobility because these joints bear the greatest load and are most prone to strain in a push‑up.  
- Keep the movements **dynamic**, **controlled**, and **repetitive** (8–12 reps per drill) to achieve the physiological benefits without sacrificing strength.  
- Avoid common pitfalls: skipping wrist work, static stretching before activity, rushing repetitions, and neglecting thoracic mobility.  

By committing to this short, focused warm‑up before each push‑up session, you lay the foundation for safe, effective training and set yourself up for steady progress toward stronger, healthier push‑ups.

modules.title: 3. Core and Scapular Stability Foundations
modules.content:
## Why a Solid Core and Stable Shoulder Blades Are the Secret to a Good Push‑Up  

Imagine you’re at the gym, ready to try your first push‑up. You drop into the **Starting Position**, lower your chest toward the floor, and push back up. As you straighten your arms, your hips suddenly dip, and the lower back arches. The movement feels awkward, and you’re left wondering why you can’t keep a straight line.  

The culprit is often the same: **insufficient core tension** and **unstable scapular control**. Even if the arm muscles are ready, a wobbly mid‑section or “floppy” shoulder blades will break the chain of force that makes a push‑up efficient and safe. This chapter gives you the foundation you need—training the core and the shoulder‑blade (scapular) system so that every push‑up starts from a rock‑solid base.

---

## 1. The Core: More Than “Abs”  

### 1.1 What the “Core” Actually Means  

When we talk about the **core**, we’re not just referring to the “abs” you see in the mirror. The core is a cylinder of muscles that wraps around your torso, linking the lower body to the upper body. It includes:

- **Rectus abdominis** (the “six‑pack” muscle)  
- **External and internal obliques** (sides of the waist)  
- **Transverse abdominis** (deep “corset” muscle)  
- **Erector spinae** (lower‑back extensors)  
- **Multifidus** (small stabilizers next to the spine)  

These muscles work together to create **intra‑abdominal pressure** and to keep the spine neutral—both are essential for a stable push‑up.

### 1.2 How Core Tension Supports the Push‑Up  

During the **Descent (Eccentric Phase)** and **Ascent (Concentric Phase)** of a push‑up, the core must:

1. **Prevent the hips from sagging** (which would shift the load to the lower back).  
2. **Stop the pelvis from tilting upward** (which would over‑activate the glutes and hinder the chest muscles).  
3. **Maintain a straight line** from head to heels, allowing the **Pectoralis Major**, **Triceps Brachii**, and **Anterior Deltoid** to work efficiently.  

Think of the core as the “rigid bar” that the upper and lower body push against. If the bar bends, the force you generate in your arms is wasted.

---

## 2. Mastering the Plank Hold  

The **plank** is the gold‑standard test for core stability. Mastering a proper plank gives you the confidence that your torso can stay rigid while the arms do the work.

### 2.1 Alignment Checklist  

| Body Part | Desired Position | Cue |
|-----------|------------------|-----|
| Head      | Neutral, eyes looking a few inches ahead | “Keep your chin tucked, but don’t look down.” |
| Shoulders | Directly over elbows (if forearm plank) or hands (if high plank) | “Shoulder blades should be proud, not hunched.” |
| Spine     | One straight line from ears to heels | “Imagine a string pulling the crown of your head toward the floor.” |
| Hips      | Neither high nor low; in line with shoulders and ankles | “Squeeze your glutes lightly to keep hips level.” |
| Knees/Feet| Straight, legs together or slightly apart | “Feet hip‑width apart for stability.” |

### 2.2 Step‑by‑Step Plank Drill  

1. **Start on your hands and knees** (tabletop position).  
2. **Place forearms on the floor**, elbows under shoulders.  
3. **Tuck the toes**, lift the knees, and extend the legs so your body forms a straight line.  
4. **Engage the core**:  
   - Draw the belly button toward the spine (activates transverse abdominis).  
   - Slightly lift the rib cage—don’t let the chest collapse.  
5. **Hold for 10 seconds** while maintaining alignment.  
6. **Rest 30 seconds**, then repeat.  

**Progression:** Add 5‑second increments each session until you can hold a solid plank for 60 seconds.  

**Common Errors & Fixes**

- **Sagging hips** → *Engage glutes and pull the belly button in.*  
- **Piking (hips too high)** → *Press the forearms into the floor and gently lower the hips.*  
- **Shoulder shrug** → *Roll the shoulders down and back; think about “pinching” a pencil between the shoulder blades.*  

### 2.3 Quick “Core‑Activation” Warm‑Up (2 minutes)

| Exercise | Duration | Key Cue |
|----------|----------|---------|
| Dead‑Bug (lying on back, opposite arm/leg extension) | 30 s | “Keep the low back glued to the floor.” |
| Bird‑Dog (from tabletop) | 30 s each side | “Extend opposite arm and leg, keep hips level.” |
| Hollow‑Hold (lying on back, shoulders and legs lifted) | 30 s | “Squeeze the lower abs, create a slight “boat” shape.” |

These mini‑exercises prime the core before you attempt a full plank or push‑up.

---

## 3. Scapular Stability: The Shoulder Blade’s Role  

### 3.1 Defining Scapular Movements  

- **Scapular Retraction** – pulling the shoulder blades toward each other (think “pinching” a pencil between them).  
- **Scapular Protraction** – sliding the shoulder blades away from each other (as when you round forward).  

Both motions are controlled by a group of muscles, most notably the **Rhomboids**, **Middle Trapezius**, and **Serratus Anterior**. In a push‑up, the scapula must **protract** as you lower your chest (allowing the shoulders to move forward) and **retract** as you push back up (bringing the shoulder blades together for stability).

### 3.2 Why Scapular Control Matters  

If the scapula “wobbles” or drifts, the **Anterior Deltoid** and **Serratus Anterior** can become over‑worked, leading to shoulder pain. Stable scapular motion ensures that the force from the **Pectoralis Major** is transferred efficiently through the shoulder joint.

### 3.3 Scapular Retraction & Protraction Drills  

#### 3.3.1 Wall Slides (Retraction Focus)

1. **Stand with back, hips, and head against a wall**; arms at 90° (goal‑post position).  
2. **Press the forearms into the wall**, squeezing the shoulder blades together.  
3. **Slide the arms upward** while maintaining contact.  
4. **Return** to the start, keeping the shoulder blades retracted throughout.  

*Reps:* 2 sets of 10.  

#### 3.3.2 Scapular Push‑Ups (Protraction/Retraction Cycle)

1. **Assume a high‑plank** (hands under shoulders, body straight).  
2. **Without bending the elbows**, let the chest sink as the shoulder blades **retract** (moving the shoulder girdle toward the spine).  
3. **Reverse the motion**, pushing the chest away as the shoulder blades **protract**.  

*Reps:* 2 sets of 8–10 cycles.  

#### 3.3.3 Band Pull‑Apart (Both Directions)

1. **Grab a light resistance band** with both hands, arms extended at shoulder height.  
2. **Pull the band apart**, focusing on squeezing the shoulder blades together (retraction).  
3. **Release slowly**, allowing the band to return while the scapula protracts.  

*Reps:* 2 sets of 12.  

### 3.4 Cue Checklist for Scapular Control  

- **“Lift the elbows”** – encourages upward rotation of the scapula for protraction.  
- **“Squeeze the shoulder blades together”** – reinforces retraction.  
- **“Keep the ribs down”** – prevents excess elevation that can destabilize the shoulder.  

---

## 4. Putting Core and Scapular Work Together  

### 4.1 How Core Tension Reinforces Scapular Stability  

When the core is **braced**, the torso acts as a rigid platform. This stability reduces unnecessary movement of the rib cage, allowing the **Serratus Anterior** to focus on controlled scapular protraction rather than compensating for a “wobbly” mid‑section. In other words, a tight core **locks** the lower spine, freeing the shoulder blades to move smoothly.

### 4.2 Integrated Mini‑Routine (10‑Minute Daily Practice)

| Exercise | Duration | Focus |
|----------|----------|-------|
| **Plank Hold** | 30 s | Core alignment |
| **Scapular Push‑Ups** | 8 cycles | Shoulder‑blade control |
| **Dead‑Bug** | 30 s | Core activation |
| **Wall Slides** | 10 reps | Scapular retraction |
| **Plank Hold** | 30 s | Reinforce core after scapular work |
| **Band Pull‑Apart** | 12 reps | Combined scapular strength |

*Tip:* Perform the routine 3–4 times per week. As the plank hold improves, increase the duration by 5 seconds each session. When the scapular drills feel easy, move to a slightly heavier band or add a **kneeling scapular push‑up** variation (knees on the ground) to increase load.

### 4.3 Checklist Before Advancing to Hand Placement  

- **Can you hold a plank** with neutral spine for at least 45 seconds?  
- **Do you feel control** over scapular retraction and protraction during the scapular push‑up drill?  
- **Is your lower back** flat (no arch) when you engage the core?  

If the answer is “yes” to all three, you’re ready to move on to **Hand Placement and Body Alignment** (the next chapter). If not, keep revisiting the drills until the cues become second nature.

---

## 5. Frequently Asked Questions  

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| *Do I need a mat for the plank?* | A thin yoga mat adds comfort, but a firm floor works fine. The key is a stable surface that doesn’t compress under your weight. |
| *Can I do the plank on my knees?* | Yes, use a **kneeling plank** as a regression. Focus on keeping the hips level and core engaged; the benefits are the same, just less load. |
| *What if my shoulders hurt during scapular push‑ups?* | Reduce the range of motion: perform the movement in a smaller arc, and double‑check that you’re not shrugging the shoulders upward. |
| *How often should I train core and scapular stability?* | 3‑4 sessions per week is sufficient for beginners. Overtraining can lead to fatigue and poor form. |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Core tension is the foundation** that keeps the body in a straight line during a push‑up, preventing hip sag or arch.  
- **Scapular retraction and protraction** are the controlled movements of the shoulder blades that allow the chest to lower and rise smoothly.  
- **Plank holds** provide a measurable way to gauge core stability; aim for at least 45 seconds of perfect form before progressing.  
- **Scapular drills** (wall slides, scapular push‑ups, band pull‑apart) teach the shoulder blades to move deliberately, reducing the risk of shoulder strain.  
- **Integrating core and scapular work** in a short daily routine builds the coordination needed for a safe, efficient push‑up.  

With a solid core and stable shoulder blades, you’ll find that the “straight line” you struggled to maintain is now a natural, effortless posture—ready for the next step in your push‑up journey.

modules.title: 4. Hand Placement and Body Alignment
modules.content:
## Setting the Stage: Why Hand Placement Matters  

Imagine you’re on a busy park bench, watching a friend breeze through ten perfect push‑ups while you struggle to keep your hips from sagging. The difference isn’t just in strength – it’s also in where the hands are placed and how the body is aligned. A subtle shift of a few centimeters can turn a push‑up from a joint‑friendly starter into a painful strain, or conversely, make it dramatically harder and more rewarding.  

Understanding hand width, finger orientation, and the line that runs from head to heels gives you control over **difficulty**, **muscle emphasis**, and **safety**. This chapter breaks those variables down, shows you how to find the optimal position for a beginner, and equips you with simple cues to fix common alignment errors.

---

## 1. Hand Width – The Foundation of Your Push‑Up  

### 1.1 The “Standard” Shoulder‑Width Position  

The most widely recommended starting point is **shoulder‑width hand placement**. To locate it:  

1. Stand upright, extend your arms straight out in front of you, and place your palms on a wall.  
2. Bring your hands together until the **inner edges of your forearms** are aligned with the **outer edges of your shoulders**.  
3. Transfer that distance onto the floor; your hands should now be roughly the width of your shoulders.

When you adopt this width, the **primary movers**—the **pectoralis major**, **triceps brachii**, and **anterior deltoid**—share the load evenly. It also respects the natural range of motion of the shoulder joint, reducing stress on the rotator cuff.

### 1.2 Wider Variations – When to Go Broader  

A **wider hand placement** (hands farther apart than shoulder width) shifts emphasis toward the **chest muscles** and reduces the contribution of the triceps. It also **increases the lever arm**, making the movement **harder** because the torso has to travel a longer distance horizontally.

Typical wider positions:  

| Hand Distance | Effect on Muscles | Difficulty Change |
|---------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| 1.25 × shoulder width | More chest activation, less triceps | Slightly harder |
| 1.5 × shoulder width | Chest‑dominant, shoulders work harder for stability | Noticeably harder |
| >1.5 × shoulder width | Primarily chest, high shoulder stress | Advanced level (not recommended for beginners) |

**When to try it:**  
- After you can comfortably perform 12–15 standard push‑ups with good form.  
- If you want to develop a broader chest or add variety to your routine.  

**Caution for beginners:**  
- Wider hands increase the demand on the **shoulder joint** and can aggravate existing shoulder impingement.  
- Start with a modest increase (≈ 10 % wider) and evaluate comfort before progressing.

### 1.3 Narrow (Close‑Grip) Placement  

A **narrow hand position** (hands closer together than shoulder width) places a greater load on the **triceps brachii** and the **inner portion of the chest**. It shortens the lever arm, making the push‑up **easier** for the chest but **harder** for the triceps.

Typical narrow positions:  

- **Hands directly under the chest** (about 6–8 cm apart).  
- **Diamond shape** (thumbs and index fingers touching) – a classic triceps‑focused variation.

**When to try it:**  
- After mastering the standard width and looking to strengthen the triceps.  
- If you experience discomfort in the shoulders when using a wider grip.

**Safety tip:** Keep the wrists in a neutral position (see §2) to avoid excess strain on the wrist joint.

---

## 2. Finger Position – The Unsung Hero of Wrist Health  

### 2.1 Flat‑Palm vs. Fist vs. Fingertip  

The orientation of your fingers influences **wrist angle**, **load distribution**, and **grip stability**. Three common options are:

| Position | Wrist Angle | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------------|------|------|
| **Flat palm** (fingers pointing forward) | Slight extension (~ 0‑10°) | Natural, easy for most people | May cause discomfort if wrists lack mobility |
| **Fist** (knuckles on the floor) | Neutral wrist | Reduces wrist extension stress | Less surface area, may feel unstable |
| **Fingertip** (balls of the fingers on the floor) | Slight flexion (~ ‑10°) | Increases forearm activation, good for grip strength | Can be hard on finger joints for beginners |

**Beginner recommendation:** Start with a **flat‑palm** placement, ensuring the wrist stays within a comfortable range of motion. If you feel a “pinching” sensation, gently work on wrist mobility (covered in Chapter 2) before progressing.

### 2.2 Spreading the Fingers  

Even when using a flat palm, the **spacing of the fingers** matters. A **slight splay** (fingers spread 2–3 cm apart) creates a broader base, improving balance and reducing the chance of the hand rolling outward during the descent.

**Cue:** “Spread your fingers like you’re trying to hold a small ball between each pair.”

### 2.3 The “Finger‑Lock” Cue for Stability  

For those who find the hands slipping, a simple cue is to **press the thumb against the index finger**, creating a “finger‑lock.” This does not change the hand width but gives a firmer grip on the floor, especially on smoother surfaces.

---

## 3. The Body Line – Maintaining a Neutral Spine  

### 3.1 What Is a Neutral Spine?  

A **neutral spine** means the natural curves of the back—cervical (neck), thoracic (upper back), and lumbar (lower back)—are **preserved**. In a push‑up, this translates to a straight line from the **head** through the **heels**.  

Recall from **Core and Scapular Stability Foundations** that the **core muscles** (abs, obliques, deep spinal stabilizers) act like a “belt” holding the spine in place. When the belt loosens, the spine either **sags** (lumbar hyperextension) or **pokes up** (lumbar flexion), both of which compromise safety and efficiency.

### 3.2 How to Feel the Alignment  

1. **Head Position** – Keep the neck in line with the spine; imagine a string pulling the crown of your head toward the ceiling.  
2. **Shoulder Position** – Scapulae (shoulder blades) should be **retracted** (pulled slightly together) and **depressed** (downward), a posture reinforced by the serratus anterior.  
3. **Hip Position** – Engage the **gluteus maximus** lightly to prevent the hips from lifting.  
4. **Heel Position** – Press through the heels, not the toes, to keep the line straight.

**Simple Test:** From a standing position, place a **tape measure** on the floor from the back of the head to the heels. When you get into the push‑up position, the tape should remain taut without any visible “dip” or “arch.”

### 3.3 Common Alignment Errors  

| Error | Description | Why It Happens | Immediate Correction |
|-------|-------------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Hip Sag** | Lower back drops, creating a “U” shape | Weak core activation or fatigue | **Cue:** “Pull your belly button toward your spine.” Engage the abdominal wall before each rep. |
| **Hip Pikes** | Hips rise, forming a “V” shape | Overactive glutes or lack of core tension | **Cue:** “Squeeze your glutes lightly, but keep the body straight.” |
| **Head Droop** | Chin tucks toward the floor, causing neck flexion | Looking down for balance | **Cue:** “Look a few inches ahead of your hands; keep the neck neutral.” |
| **Shoulder Protraction** (scapular winging) | Shoulder blades push outward, exposing the ribs | Inadequate serratus anterior activation | **Cue:** “Push the floor away with your hands, spreading the shoulder blades apart.” |

### 3.4 The “Wall Check” Alignment Drill  

1. Stand about a foot from a wall, facing it.  
2. Place your hands on the floor at shoulder width, fingers spread.  
3. Perform a push‑up while keeping your **chin** a few inches from the wall.  
4. If the wall touches the back of your torso before your chest reaches the floor, you’re **hip‑sagging**. Adjust by tightening the core.  

Repeating this drill for a few minutes each training session builds proprioceptive awareness of the correct body line.

---

## 4. Putting It All Together – A Step‑by‑Step Blueprint  

### 4.1 The Setup Checklist  

| Item | What to Do | How to Verify |
|------|------------|---------------|
| **Hand Width** | Place hands at shoulder width (or chosen variation). | Measure with a tape or use the “forearm‑shoulder” method described earlier. |
| **Finger Position** | Flat palm, fingers slightly spread. | Feel the base of the hand touching the floor evenly. |
| **Wrist Angle** | Keep wrist neutral (0‑10° extension). | Gently bend the wrist forward; it should feel comfortable, not forced. |
| **Scapular Position** | Retract and depress shoulder blades. | Imagine “pinching” a pencil between shoulder blades. |
| **Core Activation** | Draw belly button toward spine, engage glutes lightly. | Perform a “vacuum” breath for a moment; you should feel tension in the mid‑abdomen. |
| **Head Alignment** | Look a few inches ahead of the hands, keep neck neutral. | Check that the line from ear to shoulder to hip is straight. |
| **Heel Contact** | Press through heels, not toes. | Feel the weight shift toward the back of the foot. |

Run through this list **once** before each set. Over time, the cues become automatic.

### 4.2 Sample Beginner Routine  

| Set | Reps | Hand Width | Finger Position | Focus Cue |
|-----|------|------------|-----------------|-----------|
| 1 | 8 | Shoulder‑width | Flat palm, spread fingers | “Neutral spine, hips level.” |
| 2 | 8 | Shoulder‑width + 10 % | Flat palm, spread fingers | “Pull belly button in.” |
| 3 | 6 | Shoulder‑width | Flat palm, finger‑lock | “Keep shoulders down, eyes forward.” |

Rest **60–90 seconds** between sets. As you become comfortable, you can add a **wider** set or a **close‑grip** set, following the same checklist.

---

## 5. Troubleshooting Alignment Problems  

### 5.1 “My hips keep sinking”  

- **Root cause:** Core muscles not sufficiently engaged.  
- **Fix:** Before each rep, perform a **“dead‑bug”** activation: lie on your back, lift opposite arm and leg, then press the lower back into the floor. Transfer that tension to the push‑up position.  

### 5.2 “My wrists hurt”  

- **Root cause:** Excessive wrist extension or lack of mobility.  
- **Fix:** Use a **fist** or **knuckle** placement temporarily, and incorporate **wrist flexor/extensor stretches** from Chapter 2.  

### 5.3 “My shoulders feel tight”  

- **Root cause:** Scapular protraction or insufficient serratus activation.  
- **Fix:** Add a **scapular push‑up** warm‑up: from a plank, keep arms straight and move only the shoulder blades, squeezing them together then spreading them apart. This primes the serratus anterior for the main set.  

### 5.4 “I’m wobbling side‑to‑side”  

- **Root cause:** Imbalance in core stabilizers or uneven hand placement.  
- **Fix:** Re‑measure hand distance, ensure the floor is even, and practice **single‑leg holds** (lift one foot off the ground) to improve stability.

---

## 6. Progression Pathway – From Beginner to Intermediate  

1. **Standard (Shoulder‑Width) Push‑Up** – Master alignment and breathing.  
2. **Slightly Wider (≈ 10 % beyond shoulder width)** – Increases chest activation, still safe for beginners.  
3. **Close‑Grip (Triceps‑Focused)** – Emphasizes triceps, useful after standard push‑ups are comfortable.  
4. **Diamond Push‑Up** – Advanced close‑grip, adds forearm and wrist strength.  
5. **Wide Push‑Up (> 1.5 × shoulder width)** – Requires strong shoulder stability; only attempt after consistent shoulder health.  

Each step should be held for **minimum 2 weeks** with proper form before moving on.

---

## 7. Frequently Asked Questions  

**Q: Can I place my hands on an elevated surface (e.g., a bench) to make push‑ups easier?**  
A: Yes. Elevating the hands reduces the percentage of body weight you lift, but it also changes the angle of the shoulder joint. Keep the same hand‑width principles and ensure the bench is stable.

**Q: Should my fingers point forward or outward?**  
A: For beginners, pointing forward (standard flat palm) is safest. As you progress, a slight outward angle (≈ 15°) can help open the chest, but only if your shoulders feel comfortable.

**Q: Is it okay to let my hips rise a little during the ascent?**  
A: No. Any hip elevation indicates a loss of core tension and reduces the effectiveness of the exercise. Focus on maintaining the neutral spine throughout both descent and ascent.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Hand width** determines muscle emphasis and difficulty: shoulder‑width is the safest baseline; wider hands increase chest load and difficulty; narrow hands focus on triceps.  
- **Finger position** and slight finger spread promote wrist health and stability; flat‑palm is the beginner‑friendly default.  
- A **neutral spine**—head, shoulders, hips, and heels in one straight line—is essential for safe, effective push‑ups.  
- Common alignment errors (hip sag, hip pike, head droop, scapular winging) can be corrected with simple cues: engage the core, keep shoulders retracted, maintain a neutral neck, and lightly squeeze the glutes.  
- Use the **setup checklist** before each set, practice the **wall‑check drill**, and progress gradually through wider or narrower hand placements only after mastering form.  

By mastering hand placement and body alignment, you lay the groundwork for every push‑up variation that follows, ensuring strength gains come without injury.

modules.title: 5. Wall Push-Up – The First Progression
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Moment: The Kitchen Counter Coach  

Imagine you’re standing in front of the kitchen sink, coffee brewing, the kids’ backpacks hanging on the hook, and you feel a twinge of stiffness in your shoulders after a night of restless sleep. You glance at the wall, notice the empty space just a foot or two away, and decide to “fit in” a quick set of push‑ups while the water heats. Within minutes you’ve completed three solid repetitions, felt a gentle activation in your chest and triceps, and earned a small confidence boost that carries you through the rest of the morning.  

That brief, everyday scenario captures the power of the **wall push‑up**—the most accessible entry point to the push‑up movement pattern. It’s the first progression that lets you practice the full motion without the fear of falling, while still engaging the key muscle groups you’ll rely on later. Let’s break down exactly how to turn that spontaneous moment into a purposeful, repeatable practice.

---

## 1. Why the Wall Push‑Up Is the Ideal First Step  

* **Safety first** – The wall provides an immovable “handrail” that eliminates the risk of dropping to the floor.  
* **Movement pattern rehearsal** – Even though the angle is altered, you still perform the same **Starting Position → Descent (eccentric phase) → Ascent (concentric phase)** sequence introduced in Chapter 1.  
* **Scalable intensity** – By adjusting the distance from the wall or the angle of your body, you can make the exercise easier or harder, preparing you for the upcoming **inclined** and **knee** variations.  
* **Confidence builder** – Mastery of the wall push‑up gives you a concrete milestone to celebrate, reinforcing the habit of regular practice.

---

## 2. Preparing the Space and Your Body  

### 2.1 Choose a Stable Wall  

* Look for a flat, vertical surface free of cracks or protruding fixtures.  
* Ensure the floor beneath is non‑slippery; a rubber mat or carpet works well.  

### 2.2 Position Your Hands – Re‑Applying Chapter 4  

1. **Hand width** – Place your palms shoulder‑width apart, fingers pointing upward or slightly outward (≈10°).  
2. **Grip** – Keep a relaxed “soft” grip; the wall will support the load, so you don’t need to clench.  
3. **Alignment** – Your wrists should stay directly under your elbows, avoiding any “flaring” that would stress the wrist joint.  

### 2.3 Set Your Feet  

* Stand about **12–18 inches (30–45 cm)** away from the wall. The exact distance determines the difficulty: the closer you are, the less body weight you must move.  
* Feet hip‑width apart, toes pointing forward.  
* Slightly bend the knees to maintain a stable base; this also engages the **Gluteus Maximus** for better hip stability.  

### 2.4 Engage Core and Scapular Stabilizers  

Before you even begin the motion, activate the **Core Muscles** and **Serratus Anterior** (the “scapular stabilizers”) as described in **Core and Scapular Stability Foundations**. A quick cue: “Pull your belly button toward your spine and gently push your shoulder blades away from each other.” This prepares the torso for a rigid **Alignment** throughout the exercise.

---

## 3. Step‑by‑Step Execution  

Below is a concise, repeatable sequence you can mentally cue as you move through each rep.

| Phase | Cue | Key Sensations |
|-------|-----|----------------|
| **Starting Position** | “Press palms into the wall, chest out, shoulders down, core tight.” | Shoulders are depressed (away from ears); chest is slightly lifted; spine remains neutral. |
| **Descent (Eccentric)** | “Bend elbows, slide toward the wall, keep body straight.” | Elbows stay close to the torso (≈45° angle); you feel a stretch in the **Pectoralis Major** and **Anterior Deltoid**. |
| **Bottom** | “Stop when your nose is a fingertip away from the wall.” | Maintain a straight line from head to heels; no sagging hips or rounding shoulders. |
| **Ascent (Concentric)** | “Push through the palms, straighten elbows, return to start.” | Engage **Triceps Brachii** and **Chest** to drive the movement; core remains braced. |

### 3.1 Detailed Breakdown  

1. **Take a deep breath** and brace your core.  
2. **Press your palms** firmly into the wall, creating a steady base.  
3. **Shift your weight forward** slightly, allowing the shoulders to move into a comfortable, slightly protracted position (activate the serratus).  
4. **Begin the descent** by bending the elbows, keeping them tucked close to the sides of your ribcage.  
5. **Pause** when your chest is within 1–2 inches of the wall (your chosen “bottom”).  
6. **Exhale** as you push the wall away, straightening the elbows and returning to the starting position.  

Maintain **neutral spine** throughout—no excessive lumbar arch or rounded back. If you feel your hips dropping, re‑engage the glutes and core.

---

## 4. Counting Repetitions While Preserving Form  

### 4.1 The Rhythm Method  

1. **Inhale** during the descent (2‑second count).  
2. **Hold** briefly at the bottom (1‑second pause).  
3. **Exhale** during the ascent (2‑second count).  

This 5‑second cycle helps you keep a **steady cadence**, reducing the temptation to rush and lose alignment.

### 4.2 Repetition Targets for Beginners  

| Session | Sets | Reps per Set | Rest |
|--------|------|--------------|------|
| **Day 1** | 3 | 8–10 | 60 s |
| **Day 3** | 3 | 10–12 | 45 s |
| **Day 5** | 4 | 12–15 | 45 s |

Start with the lower end of the rep range. If you cannot maintain proper **Alignment** for the full set, stop early, rest, and resume once you feel stable again. Quality outweighs quantity.

### 4.3 Self‑Check Checklist (Perform After Each Set)  

- **Shoulders**: Are they still down and back?  
- **Spine**: Is the line from head to heels straight?  
- **Core**: Does the belly feel engaged, not relaxed?  
- **Elbows**: Are they staying close to the body, not flaring outward?  

If any answer is “no,” reduce the distance from the wall or lower the rep count until the form returns to neutral.

---

## 5. Transitioning to an Inclined Surface  

Once the wall push‑up feels comfortable for three consecutive sessions, it’s time to increase the load by moving to an **inclined surface** (e.g., sturdy kitchen counter, low bench, or step). This shift reduces the angle between your torso and the floor, demanding more of the same muscles while still offering a safety net.

### 5.1 Selecting the Right Height  

| Surface Height | Approximate Angle (from vertical) | Difficulty |
|----------------|-----------------------------------|------------|
| 12 in (30 cm) | ~75° | Easy |
| 18 in (45 cm) | ~60° | Moderate |
| 24 in (60 cm) | ~45° | Challenging |

A good rule of thumb: **If you can complete 12 reps with perfect form, move up one level.**  

### 5.2 The Inclined Push‑Up Protocol  

1. **Place hands** on the edge of the chosen surface, shoulder‑width apart.  
2. **Step back** until your body forms a straight line; the further you step, the more horizontal the line becomes.  
3. **Engage core** and **scapular stabilizers** as before.  
4. **Perform the descent** by bending elbows, aiming to bring your chest within a few centimeters of the surface.  
5. **Press back** to the starting position, maintaining the same cues used for the wall version.  

### 5.3 Progression Timeline  

| Week | Goal | Details |
|------|------|---------|
| **1–2** | Master wall push‑up | 3 × 10‑12 reps, perfect form |
| **3** | Introduce 12‑in inclined surface | 2 × 8‑10 reps, focus on alignment |
| **4** | Increase to 18‑in surface | 2 × 6‑8 reps, maintain core bracing |
| **5+** | Alternate wall & inclined sets | Mix to build endurance and confidence |

---

## 6. Sample Beginner Routine  

Below is a ready‑to‑use program that blends the wall and inclined variations, ensuring progressive overload while reinforcing technique.

| Day | Exercise | Sets | Reps | Rest |
|-----|----------|------|------|------|
| **Mon** | Wall Push‑Up | 3 | 10 | 60 s |
| **Tue** | Rest or Light Mobility | – | – | – |
| **Wed** | Inclined Push‑Up (12 in) | 3 | 8 | 60 s |
| **Thu** | Rest or Light Mobility | – | – | – |
| **Fri** | Wall Push‑Up | 3 | 12 | 45 s |
| **Sat** | Optional Light Cardio | – | – | – |
| **Sun** | Rest | – | – | – |

**Tips**  

* Keep a **training log**: note distance from wall, rep count, perceived effort, and any form breakdowns.  
* Use a **mirror** or record yourself on phone to verify alignment.  
* Prioritize **breathing**—inhale on descent, exhale on ascent—to maintain a rhythmic pattern.

---

## 7. Troubleshooting Common Hurdles  

| Issue | Likely Cause | Fix |
|-------|--------------|-----|
| **Hips sagging** | Core not engaged, glutes relaxed | Perform a **dead‑bug** drill (Chapter 3) before each set; cue “push belly button toward spine.” |
| **Shoulders creeping up** | Lack of scapular depression, fatigue | Re‑activate the **Serratus Anterior** by “pushing the wall away” before each rep; take longer rest between sets. |
| **Elbows flaring** | Over‑reaching for stability | Keep elbows at a **45° angle** relative to the torso; imagine “tucking the elbows into a book on your chest.” |
| **Unable to keep distance** | Too far from wall, making the movement too hard | Step closer until you can comfortably complete 10 reps with proper form. |

If multiple issues appear simultaneously, reduce the difficulty (move closer to the wall) and focus on one cue at a time.

---

## 8. Integrating the Wall Push‑Up Into a Larger Routine  

Even though this chapter focuses on the first progression, it’s useful to consider where the wall push‑up fits into your overall fitness plan:

* **Warm‑up** – Pair a set of wall push‑ups with shoulder mobility drills (e.g., arm circles).  
* **Strength block** – After mastering the wall version, use it as a “reset” exercise between more demanding sets (e.g., after a set of squats).  
* **Recovery** – On active‑recovery days, perform a low‑intensity wall push‑up circuit (2 × 8 reps) to maintain neuromuscular memory without taxing the muscles.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **wall push‑up** is the safest, most accessible way to practice the full push‑up movement pattern.  
- Proper **hand placement**, **body distance**, and **core/scapular engagement** are essential for maintaining alignment.  
- Use a **5‑second rhythm** (inhale‑descent, pause, exhale‑ascent) to keep form consistent while counting reps.  
- Progress to an **inclined surface** once you can perform three consecutive sessions with perfect technique; choose height based on ability to maintain alignment.  
- A structured routine—alternating wall and inclined variations—provides progressive overload and prepares you for the next step: knee push‑ups.  

By mastering the wall push‑up, you lay a solid foundation for every subsequent push‑up progression, turning everyday moments into purposeful strength‑building opportunities. Keep the wall close, stay aligned, and push forward.

modules.title: 6. Knee (Modified) Push-Up Technique
modules.content:
## From the Wall to the Floor: Why the Knee Push‑Up Is Your Next Milestone  

Imagine you’ve spent the past two weeks mastering the wall push‑up. The motion feels smoother, your chest and triceps fire with less effort, and you’ve already logged a few sets. Yet the floor still looks intimidating—your hands hover above the carpet, and the thought of lowering your chest all the way down feels like a leap.  

**Enter the knee (modified) push‑up.** It bridges the gap between the wall version and the full‑body push‑up by shifting more of your body weight onto your hands while still giving your core and lower‑body a supportive base. In other words, it lets you practice the **descent (eccentric phase)** and **ascent (concentric phase)** with a more manageable load, reinforcing the alignment principles you learned in Chapter 4 and the core‑stability cues from Chapter 3.

> *“The knee push‑up is the ‘training wheels’ for a standard push‑up—once you can keep a straight line from knees to head, the transition to full‑body becomes a matter of confidence rather than strength.”*  

---

## 1. Setting Up for Success  

### 1.1 Choose a Stable Surface  

- **Floor type:** A non‑slippery surface such as a rubber mat, carpet, or hardwood with a yoga mat works best.  
- **Space:** Ensure you have at least a 3‑foot radius around you; you’ll need room for hand placement adjustments later.  

### 1.2 Adopt the Starting Position  

1. **Knees on the ground** – Sit back onto your heels so that your thighs are vertical and your calves rest flat.  
2. **Hands in line with shoulders** – Place your palms flat, fingers spread slightly, directly under (or just slightly outside) your shoulders. This mirrors the hand placement discussed in Chapter 4.  
3. **Body line:** Imagine a straight rod running from the **knees** through the hips, spine, shoulders, and head. Your **core muscles** (abs and obliques) should be gently engaged to prevent sagging or piking.  

> **Tip:** Perform a quick “plank check”—lift one hand off the ground briefly. If your hips dip or your lower back arches, you’ve lost alignment. Re‑engage the core and retry.  

### 1.3 Warm‑up Recap  

Before you begin, repeat the mobility drills from Chapter 2 (arm circles, thoracic rotations, and wrist flexor stretches). A warm‑up primes the **pectoralis major**, **triceps brachii**, and **serratus anterior**, reducing the risk of strain when you lower your chest toward the floor.  

---

## 2. Executing the Knee Push‑Up  

### 2.1 The Descent (Eccentric Phase)  

1. **Inhale** as you begin to lower your chest.  
2. **Elbow angle:** Aim for a 45‑degree angle between the upper arm and torso—this protects the shoulder joint and engages the **anterior deltoid** efficiently.  
3. **Depth:** Continue until your chest is a few centimeters above the floor (or until your elbows reach a 90‑degree angle). If you’re new, stopping at the point where your forearms are parallel to the ground is acceptable.  

### 2.2 The Ascent (Concentric Phase)  

1. **Exhale** and push through the palms, straightening the elbows.  
2. **Maintain the straight line:** As you press up, keep the hips level; avoid lifting the hips (which would shift weight to the glutes) or letting them drop.  
3. **Finish:** Return to the starting position with the shoulders directly over the hands, ready for the next repetition.  

### 2.3 Breathing Rhythm  

| Phase | Action | Breathing |
|-------|--------|-----------|
| Descent | Lower chest | Inhale |
| Ascent | Press up | Exhale |

A consistent breathing pattern not only supplies oxygen to working muscles but also helps you stay **core‑stable** throughout the movement.  

---

## 3. Hand Placement Variations to Gradually Increase Difficulty  

Once you can perform 10‑12 quality reps with the standard hand position, it’s time to tweak the placement to add challenge and stimulate the muscles differently.  

| Variation | Hand Position | Primary Effect |
|-----------|---------------|----------------|
| **Narrow** | Hands directly under the chest, elbows close to the body | Increases load on the **triceps brachii** and **inner chest** |
| **Wide** | Hands wider than shoulder width, elbows at ~45° | Emphasizes the **pectoralis major** and stretches the shoulders |
| **Staggered** | One hand slightly forward, the other back (≈6‑8 inches) | Engages stabilizing muscles, improves unilateral strength |
| **Fingertip** | Balance on fingertips instead of palms | Boosts wrist stability and forearm activation |

**Progression tip:** Start each session with the “standard” placement for the first set, then rotate through one of the variations for subsequent sets. This systematic approach respects the objective of “adjusting hand placement to increase difficulty gradually.”  

---

## 4. Building a Routine: Reps, Sets, and Quality  

### 4.1 Sample Beginner Session  

| Set | Reps | Hand Placement | Rest |
|-----|------|----------------|------|
| 1 | 8–10 | Standard | 60 s |
| 2 | 6–8 | Wide | 60 s |
| 3 | 6–8 | Narrow | 90 s |

- **Why this structure?** The first set establishes a baseline of **quality** (full range of motion, proper alignment). Subsequent sets introduce variation while allowing enough rest for the **core muscles** to maintain stability.  

### 4.2 Quality Over Quantity  

- **Full range of motion:** Each rep should reach the prescribed depth before pressing up.  
- **Control:** Avoid “bouncing” at the bottom; a controlled descent maximizes eccentric loading.  
- **Alignment check:** After every 5 reps, pause briefly, look at your body line, and correct any hip sag or pike.  

If you find yourself compromising form to hit rep targets, reduce the number of reps and focus on perfect execution.  

---

## 5. Tracking Progress: The Simple Log  

A concrete, realistic way to monitor improvement is a **push‑up log**. Here’s a minimalistic template you can keep in a notebook or on your phone:

| Date | Set 1 (Reps / Quality) | Set 2 (Reps / Hand) | Set 3 (Reps / Hand) | Notes |
|------|------------------------|---------------------|---------------------|-------|
| 08‑01| 9 / ✅ | 7 / Wide | 6 / Narrow | Felt strong, slight wrist fatigue |
| 08‑04| 10 / ✅ | 8 / Wide | 7 / Narrow | Added staggered hand placement |

- **Quality flag (✅/❌):** Mark a rep set as ✅ only if you maintained a straight line and full depth.  
- **Notes column:** Jot down any sensations (e.g., “tightness in shoulders”) or external factors (e.g., “sleepy” or “after cardio”).  

Review the log weekly. Look for trends such as increasing reps, smoother hand‑placement transitions, or reduced notes about discomfort. Those trends indicate that you’re meeting the objectives of **executing a knee push‑up with proper alignment** and **gradually increasing difficulty**.  

---

## 6. Real‑World Scenario: Sarah’s First Knee Push‑Up  

> **Profile:** Sarah, 35, works a desk job and spends 30 minutes daily on the wall push‑up. She wants to feel stronger for her upcoming hiking trip.  

1. **Initial assessment:** Sarah can comfortably perform 12 wall push‑ups with perfect form.  
2. **Transition plan:**  
   - **Week 1:** Introduce the knee push‑up, 2 sets of 8 reps, standard hand placement.  
   - **Week 2:** Add a wide‑hand set, increase to 3 sets total.  
   - **Week 3:** Incorporate a narrow‑hand set and begin tracking with the log.  
3. **Outcome:** After three weeks, Sarah’s log shows a progression from 8‑10 reps per set to 12‑14 reps, all flagged ✅. She reports reduced shoulder tightness and feels confident to attempt the first full‑body push‑up.  

Sarah’s story illustrates how the knee push‑up serves as a **structured, measurable step** toward the full‑body push‑up, reinforcing the learning goal of **tracking progress by recording reps and quality**.  

---

## 7. Safety and Common Sensations  

- **Elbow flare:** If your elbows flare out beyond 45°, you’re placing unnecessary stress on the shoulder joint. Keep them tucked slightly toward the torso.  
- **Hip sag:** A drooping pelvis indicates insufficient core activation. Engage the **gluteus maximus** lightly to help maintain a straight line.  
- **Wrist discomfort:** Adjust hand angle (rotate slightly outward) or use a small rolled towel under the palms to reduce strain.  

If pain (sharp or acute) occurs, stop immediately and reassess your form. Persistent discomfort may require consultation with a healthcare professional.  

---

## 8. When to Move On  

You’ve mastered the knee push‑up when **all three objectives** are met:

1. **Straight line** from knees to head is consistently maintained across sets.  
2. **Hand placement variations** are executed without loss of alignment.  
3. **Progress logs** show a steady increase in reps or a transition to more challenging hand positions while maintaining quality flags.  

At this point, you’re ready to graduate to the **standard full‑body push‑up** covered in Chapter 7.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The knee push‑up shifts more weight onto the hands while still offering a supportive base, making it the logical next step after wall push‑ups.  
- **Execution fundamentals:** start in a straight line from knees to head, lower chest with elbows at ~45°, press up while preserving alignment, and synchronize breathing (inhale down, exhale up).  
- Gradually increase difficulty by **adjusting hand placement** (standard → wide → narrow → staggered) and by adding more reps or sets.  
- **Track progress** with a simple log that records reps, hand placement, quality flags, and personal notes; review weekly to spot improvements.  
- Maintain **core engagement** and watch for common cues—hip sag, elbow flare, wrist discomfort—to ensure safe, effective practice.  

By consistently applying these principles, you’ll build the strength, control, and confidence needed to transition smoothly to the full‑body push‑up and beyond.

modules.title: 7. Full-Body (Standard) Push-Up Progression
modules.content:
## From Knees to Full‑Body: The Turning Point  

Imagine you’ve just mastered the knee (modified) push‑up. Your chest lowers comfortably, your core stays engaged, and you can finish a set of ten without wobbling. Yet when you try the classic, full‑body push‑up, you feel a gap in strength, a wobble in the hips, or a tendency to flare the elbows. This is the exact moment many beginners hit the “plateau” that separates a functional push‑up from a true full‑body movement.  

The good news? The transition is a matter of **adding tension, adjusting elbow angle, and mastering a few key cues**. Below is a step‑by‑step progression that takes you from the knee version you already know to a solid, standard push‑up performed with elbows at a 45‑degree angle, a rigid core, and smooth, controlled motion.

---

## 1. Assessing Readiness  

Before you attempt the full‑body version, run a quick self‑check. You should already be comfortable with the foundations covered in **Core and Scapular Stability Foundations**, **Hand Placement and Body Alignment**, and the **Knee (Modified) Push‑Up Technique**. Use the following checklist:

| ✅ Ready When… | ❌ Needs Work |
|---|---|
| You can hold a **plank** with a neutral spine for at least **30 seconds**. | Your hips sag or pike within 10 seconds. |
| You can perform **10 knee push‑ups** with correct elbow angle (≈45°) and no excessive shoulder rounding. | You feel pain in the shoulders or wrists during knee push‑ups. |
| You can maintain **scapular retraction** (shoulder blades pulled slightly together) while pressing against a wall. | Your shoulder blades slide forward or lift away from the ribs. |
| You can keep your **core braced** (imagine gently pulling your belly button toward your spine) throughout the movement. | Your lower back arches or your pelvis tilts. |

If any item is marked “❌,” revisit the earlier chapters until the skill feels solid. The full‑body push‑up builds directly on those foundations; missing a piece will make the transition feel unstable.

---

## 2. Positioning the Body  

### 2.1 Set‑Up in One Shot  

1. **Find a flat surface** – a gym mat or carpeted floor works best.  
2. **Place your hands** directly under your shoulders, slightly wider than shoulder‑width (the hand placement described in Chapter 4).  
3. **Extend your legs** behind you, feet together, toes tucked under for balance.  
4. **Engage the core**: gently draw your belly button toward your spine, activate the glutes, and keep the neck in line with the spine (no “head‑dropping”).  

### 2.2 Body Alignment Checklist  

- **Head**: eyes looking a few inches ahead, not down.  
- **Spine**: straight line from head to heels, no sagging or piking.  
- **Shoulders**: over the wrists, not drifting forward.  
- **Hips**: locked in line with the torso, not rising toward the ceiling.  

Visualize a **“straight board”** connecting your head, shoulders, hips, and heels. This mental image, borrowed from the earlier alignment concepts, will help you keep the whole body rigid throughout the movement.

---

## 3. The 45‑Degree Elbow Rule  

Why 45 degrees?  

- **Joint safety** – a 45° angle reduces stress on the shoulder joint compared with a flared‑out (90°) or too‑narrow (0°) position.  
- **Muscle activation** – it maximizes recruitment of the **pectoralis major**, **triceps brachii**, and **anterior deltoid** while still engaging the **serratus anterior** for scapular stability.  

### 3.1 Feeling the Angle  

1. Start in the set‑up position.  
2. Lower your forearms toward the floor, keeping your elbows **just inside** the line of your shoulders.  
3. Imagine a line drawn from each elbow to the center of your shoulder joint; this line should form roughly a **45° angle** with the torso.  

If you’re unsure, place a small **tape mark** on the floor a few inches out from each hand. When you lower, the elbows should point toward those marks. As you gain confidence, the marks can be removed.

---

## 4. Engaging Full‑Body Tension  

A full‑body push‑up isn’t just about the upper body. The **core**, **glutes**, and even the **quadriceps** act like a tensioned cable that keeps the spine rigid.

### 4.1 The “Brace & Squeeze” Sequence  

1. **Brace** – Take a deep breath, then exhale partially while tightening the abdominal wall (think of bracing for a punch).  
2. **Squeeze** – Simultaneously contract the glutes and engage the quadriceps. This locks the pelvis and prevents hip lift.  

### 4.2 Why It Matters  

- **Stability**: A rigid core stops the hips from sagging, which would shift the load away from the chest and onto the lower back.  
- **Efficiency**: When the body is a single, solid unit, the force you generate with the arms translates directly into upward movement.  

Practice the brace‑squeeze combo in a **static plank** for 10 seconds, then transition directly into a push‑up. The feeling of a “tight shell” should carry over.

---

## 5. The Descent (Eccentric Phase)  

A controlled descent is the cornerstone of a smooth push‑up.

1. **Inhale** as you begin to lower your chest.  
2. **Maintain the 45° elbow angle**; keep the elbows tracking in line with the forearms, not flaring out.  
3. **Lower until** your chest is about **1–2 inches** above the floor (or until your elbows reach a 90° bend).  
4. **Check tension**: core engaged, hips level, shoulders stable.  

**Tip:** Count silently to **three** while descending. If you reach the bottom before “three,” you’re moving too fast and likely losing tension.

---

## 6. The Ascent (Concentric Phase)  

The upward push mirrors the descent but adds a focus on driving through the hands.

1. **Exhale** as you press upward.  
2. **Push through the “knuckles”** – imagine the force traveling from the palm, through the wrist, up the forearm, and into the shoulder.  
3. **Keep elbows at 45°**; they should not drift outward as you straighten.  
4. **Finish with the arms fully extended**, but avoid locking the elbows (keep a slight bend to protect the joint).  

A smooth ascent should feel like **releasing a spring** that you’ve compressed during the descent. The core and glutes stay engaged the entire time; they never “relax” between phases.

---

## 7. Transition Drill: Knee‑to‑Toe Progression  

If a full‑body push‑up feels too demanding, use this three‑step drill to bridge the gap.

### 7.1 Step 1 – Elevated Hands  

- **Setup**: Place both hands on a sturdy surface (bench, step, or low wall) that is **2–4 inches** higher than the floor.  
- **Goal**: Perform the same movement pattern while your feet remain on the ground. This reduces the load on the upper body while still demanding core tension.  

### 7.2 Step 2 – Partial Toe Lift  

- **Setup**: Return to the floor, but instead of full extension, **lift the knees** just a few inches off the ground, keeping the hips level.  
- **Goal**: You’re now supporting a larger proportion of body weight than on the knees, but the reduced distance to the floor makes the movement more manageable.  

### 7.3 Step 3 – Full Toe Lift (Standard)  

- **Setup**: From the partial lift, extend the knees fully, achieving the classic straight‑body position.  
- **Goal**: Perform a full push‑up, maintaining all cues (45° elbows, rigid core, smooth tempo).  

**Progression Rule:** Move to the next step only after you can complete **10 clean repetitions** on the current step with proper form. If you struggle before reaching 10, stay on the current step and repeat the drill until strength and confidence improve.

---

## 8. Cue Checklist for a Smooth, Controlled Push‑Up  

Keep this list handy—either printed on a small card or saved on your phone. Review it before each set.

- **Hand Position**: Hands under shoulders, fingers spread for stability.  
- **Elbow Angle**: Approx. 45° from torso; elbows tracking toward the taped floor markers.  
- **Core Brace**: Belly button pulled toward spine, no sagging.  
- **Glute Squeeze**: Tighten glutes; hips stay level with shoulders.  
- **Breathing**: Inhale on descent, exhale on ascent.  
- **Tempo**: 3‑second descent, 1‑second pause (optional), 2‑second ascent.  
- **Head Alignment**: Eyes a few inches ahead, neck neutral.  
- **Foot Contact**: Toes planted firmly; weight distributed evenly across the forefoot and heel.  

Mentally rehearsing these cues before each set dramatically improves consistency, especially when fatigue sets in.

---

## 9. Building Confidence: Reps, Sets, and Rest  

### 9.1 Starting Protocol  

| Goal | Reps per Set | Sets | Rest |
|------|--------------|------|------|
| **Learning the movement** | 5–6 | 3 | 90 seconds |
| **Strength focus** | 8–10 | 3–4 | 2 minutes |
| **Endurance focus** | 12–15 | 2–3 | 1 minute |

Begin with the lower‑rep range; the emphasis is on **quality, not quantity**. As the core and upper‑body muscles adapt, increase reps gradually—no more than **2–3 additional reps** per week.

### 9.2 Tracking Progress  

- **Logbook**: Write down the number of reps, any deviations from the cue checklist, and perceived difficulty (scale 1–10).  
- **Video Review**: Record a set from the side and compare your elbow angle and spine alignment to a reference video from earlier chapters.  
- **Periodic Test**: Every two weeks, attempt a **max‑reps set** of full‑body push‑ups with perfect form. The improvement in rep count is a concrete measure of progress.

---

## 10. Putting It All Together – A Sample Session  

1. **Warm‑up** – 5 minutes of dynamic shoulder circles, cat‑cow stretches, and a 30‑second plank (from Chapter 3).  
2. **Cue Review** – Run through the cue checklist silently.  
3. **Progression Drill** – Perform **2 sets of 8 elevated‑hand push‑ups**, focusing on core tension.  
4. **Full‑Body Push‑Ups** – Aim for **3 sets of 6–8 reps** using the 45° elbow rule and the brace‑squeeze sequence.  
5. **Cool‑down** – Stretch the chest (doorway stretch) and triceps, finish with a gentle abdominal breathing exercise to release core tension.  

By structuring the session around the same cues and progression steps, the learner creates a repeatable routine that reinforces muscle memory and confidence.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Readiness matters**: Only move to the full‑body push‑up when you can hold a plank, perform knee push‑ups with proper elbow angle, and keep a rigid core.  
- **45° elbows protect the shoulders** and maximize chest, triceps, and front‑shoulder activation.  
- **Full‑body tension**—core brace, glute squeeze, and quadriceps engagement—keeps the spine neutral and transfers force efficiently.  
- **Controlled tempo** (3‑second descent, 2‑second ascent) ensures smooth, safe movement and builds strength.  
- **Transition drills** (elevated hands → partial toe lift → full toe lift) provide a graduated pathway to the standard push‑up.  
- **Cue checklist** is your on‑the‑spot safety net; review it before each set.  
- **Progressive overload** (adding reps, sets, or reducing rest) should be gradual, with an emphasis on form over volume.  

Mastering these elements transforms a beginner’s knee push‑up into a confident, full‑body push‑up performed with precision and control. Keep practicing the cues, respect the 45° elbow rule, and maintain that rigid core—your body will thank you with stronger, more functional strength.

modules.title: 8. Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
modules.content:
## Spotting the Mistakes Before They Become Habits  

Imagine Maya, a 27‑year‑old office worker, just finished her first **Full‑Body (Standard) Push‑Up Progression** from Chapter 7. She feels a burn in her chest and a sense of accomplishment—until she watches the playback on her phone. The video shows her hips dropping like a sagging bridge, elbows pointing outwards, and her head jutting forward.  

Maya’s experience is common. New push‑up practitioners often develop “bad habits” that hide behind the effort of the movement. Because the push‑up is a **compound exercise** (it involves several joints and muscle groups working together), a flaw in one segment can compromise the entire pattern, increase injury risk, and stall progress.  

The good news: each mistake has a clear, actionable fix. By learning to **recognize** the three most frequent errors—**sagging hips**, **flared elbows**, and a **broken neck**—and applying the cues and drills described below, you can train a clean, efficient push‑up from the very first repetition.

---

## 1. Sagging Hips – The “Hip Drop”  

### Why the hips drop  

A sagging‑hip push‑up usually stems from **insufficient core engagement** and **weak glute activation**. When the abdominal wall (the “belt” that keeps the spine stable) can’t hold the pelvis level, gravity pulls the lower back toward the floor, creating a “pike” shape.  

### Quick visual cue  

> **“Imagine you’re trying to stretch a taut sheet of paper from your shoulders to your knees.”**  

If the sheet sags, you know the core is not tight enough.

### Corrective cues  

| Cue | When to apply | How it feels |
|-----|---------------|--------------|
| **Brace the core** – “Pull your belly button toward your spine, as if you were bracing for a punch.” | At the start of the **Starting Position** and maintain through the **Descent** and **Ascent**. | You should feel a gentle tightening across the entire mid‑section, not a hard “suck” but a firm, active engagement. |
| **Squeeze the glutes** – “Press your hips upward, as if you’re trying to lift a small ball under your tailbone.” | Right after you set the core brace, before you begin the descent. | A subtle contraction in the buttocks that keeps the pelvis from tipping down. |
| **Feet “push”** – “Press your toes into the ground, pulling your body forward.” | Throughout the movement. | This creates a chain reaction: feet push → legs engage → hips stay level. |

### Drill: “Wall Hip Hold”
